title: Tower of ivory, house of gold
hook: poetic titles from scripture and old hymns

segments.voice: Yesterday, Loreto: the litany that calls Mary by name after name, each one answered with pray for us. Your line was many names. Which of the five did you keep? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-two.

In everyday English, an ivory tower is usually a put-down. Say someone lives in one, and you mean they're out of touch. But halfway down the Litany of Loreto, the phrase turns up as a name for a mother. Tower of ivory. House of gold. Then, without a pause, ark of the covenant, gate of heaven, morning star. Not one of these is a sentence. Not one explains itself. They are pictures, set side by side, the way someone who loves a person keeps reaching past ordinary words for a better one. Where do pictures like these come from, and why would anyone pray in them? Today's word is the first of the pair.
screen: `AN IVORY TOWER, USUALLY A PUT-DOWN.` → `HERE, A NAME FOR A MOTHER.` → `PICTURES, NOT SENTENCES.`

segments.voice: Start with the tower. It comes out of a love song. In the Canticle of Canticles, the Song of Songs, a lover praises the beloved line by line, and in the Douay-Rheims one line reads: "Thy neck as a tower of ivory." Some Jewish and Christian readers have heard this poem as being about more than two lovers: God and his people, Christ and the Church, God and the soul. Some Christian writers took its lines and gave them to Mary. So the title isn't a fresh invention. It's borrowed love poetry. Now the ivory. Ivory is rare, pale and smooth, and a tower is strong; it stands guard. Put the two together and you get something lovely and sturdy at once, a beauty that doesn't break. That's the picture the litany hands over, and it leaves you to sit with it. Then the house of gold. In the Book of Kings, Solomon's Temple is covered inside with gold, and in Exodus the ark of the covenant is overlaid with gold, inside and out. In those stories the gold isn't there for show. It marks the place where God chose to dwell. Catholics call Mary a house of gold for the same reason: she carried Christ. The house is precious because of who lives in it. Notice what that does. Each title points past her, to the one she held. Catholic teaching about Mary has its careful, exact statements; this stretch on Mary began with four of them. The litany speaks another language, the one a child uses about a mother: not a definition, but a pile of names that never quite says enough.
screen: `A LINE FROM A LOVE SONG.` · `LOVELY AND STRONG AT ONCE.` · `GOLD MARKS WHERE GOD DWELLS.` · `A CHILD'S LANGUAGE, NOT A DEFINITION.` · then, large: `THY NECK AS A TOWER OF IVORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your favorite title. Settle, and breathe. Let a few of the litany's names go by, slowly, one per breath. Mystical rose. Tower of David. Tower of ivory. House of gold. Ark of the covenant. Gate of heaven. Morning star. Notice which one makes you stop. Don't pick the cleverest. Pick the one that stays. Then hold its picture for a while: a white tower, a golden room, an open gate, a star before dawn. Ask what it shows. If you pray, you can say that one title and the litany's answer, pray for us, and let it repeat. If you don't, keep the picture in mind and let it be enough. The bell holds the time.
Tower of ivory. A title of Mary from the Litany of Loreto, borrowed from the Song of Songs: beauty and strength in one picture, with its partner, house of gold. Today's word.
Your line: poetry for a mother. Today, find one picture, not an adjective, for someone you love, and keep it, or tell them. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Litany of Loreto, with titles like Tower of Ivory and House of Gold, in parishes and at home, often after the rosary, answering each title with "pray for us."

notes: Confirm the Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of Canticle 7:4 ('Thy neck as a tower of ivory.'); KJV reads 'Thy neck is as a tower of ivory'.
The Temple's gold (3 Kings 6:20–22) and the ark overlaid with gold inside and out (Exodus 25:11) are paraphrased.

Claim that both Jewish and Christian readers have read the Song of Songs allegorically (God and Israel; Christ and the Church; God and the soul), and that some Christian writers applied its lines to Mary, is stated without names or dates. Confirm phrasing.
The modern English sense of 'ivory tower' as out of touch is stated as everyday usage, not as an etymology.
Order of titles in the practice follows the standard litany order (Mystical Rose through Morning Star); confirm.
Editor pass: 'Both Jewish and Christian readers' softened to 'Some Jewish and Christian readers' (claims rule); the Temple-gold line reworded to stay with what the stories show.
